cases.title: Exam Anxiety
cases.situation: Alex is a 20-year-old college student majoring in computer science. With final exams approaching, Alex feels an overwhelming sense of anxiety and panic, worrying constantly about failing courses and disappointing their family. They struggle to focus on studying, often procrastinate, and lose sleep over imagined scenarios of poor performance. During the day, Alex experiences tension headaches and a racing heart when thinking about exams, and feels self-critical for not being able to study effectively.
user_turns: I know I need to study for my finals, but every time I try, I get this wave of panic and my mind just goes blank or starts imagining the worst-case scenarios. I end up wasting hours just feeling guilty and paralyzed. How can I break this cycle and actually start focusing without the constant anxiety?

Thank you, that helps to hear. It's like my brain just jumps straight to "you're going to fail everything and disappoint everyone" before I've even opened a book. Breaking it into smaller chunks makes sense logically, but in the moment, that logic just disappears. I like the idea of setting really small goals—maybe just reviewing one topic at a time instead of thinking about the whole exam. And you're right, I should try to remember past times when I was stressed about something and it ended up being fine. I guess I just forget those moments when the anxiety hits. The mindfulness stuff is hard for me because my mind races so fast, but maybe if I start with just a minute of deep breathing before I study, it could help slow things down. What do you suggest if the anxious thoughts keep coming back even after I try to breathe or break things down?

Thanks, that's really helpful advice. I think the positive self-talk is something I seriously neglect—when I'm in that anxious state, my inner voice is pretty harsh, telling me I'm not prepared enough or that I'm going to mess up. I never really thought about actively fighting back with something more balanced. The journal idea is interesting too. I tend to just let the thoughts swirl around in my head, and writing them down might actually force me to see how extreme they are. Like, when I actually see "I'm going to fail and never get a job" on paper, it might look more ridiculous than it feels in my mind. I do have a question about the physical activity part—I know exercise helps, but when I'm stressed, I feel like I don't have time to work out because I "should" be studying. How do you balance that? Like, how do you convince yourself that taking 20 minutes to move your body isn't wasting time, but actually helping you study better?

That makes a lot of sense—reframing it as an investment instead of a distraction. I guess I have this all-or-nothing mindset where if I'm not sitting at my desk with my books, I'm not being productive. But you're right, if exercise actually helps me focus better afterward, then those 20 minutes aren't lost time at all—they're probably saving me from hours of staring blankly at a page. I think I could handle a short walk or even just some stretching between study sessions. Maybe I could even use it as a reward system—like if I finish reviewing one chapter, I get to take a quick walk outside before starting the next one. That might make the studying feel less like a punishment and more manageable. I appreciate you normalizing this too. Sometimes I feel like I'm the only one struggling with this, but hearing that there are actual strategies and that other people deal with similar things helps me feel less alone in it. Do you have any tips for the night before an exam? That's usually when my anxiety peaks and I can't sleep.

Thanks, that's really practical advice. I definitely fall into the trap of scrolling through my phone in bed when I'm anxious, which probably just makes things worse. I never thought about how the blue light and constant information might be keeping my brain wired when I need it to shut off. The grounding exercises sound helpful too—I tend to lie there with my heart racing, thinking about all the things I might forget on the test. Focusing on my senses might actually pull me out of that spiral. Like, maybe noticing the feeling of the blanket or the sounds in the room could anchor me enough to fall asleep. I think the preparation part is key too. A lot of my night-before panic probably comes from feeling like I haven't done enough, even if I actually have. Maybe if I make a checklist of everything I've reviewed throughout the week, I can look at it that night and have physical proof that I'm prepared. That might quiet that voice telling me I'm not ready. Thank you for all this. It's been really helpful talking through this. I feel like I actually have a plan now instead of just feeling stuck and overwhelmed.

Thank you, I really appreciate that. It helps to be reminded that I don't have to get it perfect right away—just starting somewhere is enough. I'll try to be kinder to myself through this process and actually notice when I make small progress instead of only focusing on what's left to do. Having this conversation has made me feel a lot more in control than I did when I first reached out. I'm going to try the breathing before studying, the short walks as rewards, and that grounding technique if I can't sleep before the exam. It feels good to have a plan. I might check in again if I hit a rough patch, but for now, I feel ready to give this a shot. Thanks again for listening and for all the helpful suggestions.

cases.title: Social Anxiety
cases.situation: Jordan, a 23-year-old recent graduate, has just started a new job in a corporate setting. They feel intense fear of speaking in meetings, worried that colleagues are constantly judging their every word. Jordan tends to overthink every interaction, avoiding eye contact and remaining quiet, even when they have useful input. Social gatherings at work feel exhausting, and they often leave early to avoid feeling embarrassed or scrutinized. This anxiety has started affecting their confidence and sense of belonging at the workplace.
user_turns: Ever since I started my new job, I’ve been terrified of speaking up in meetings. I constantly worry that people are judging me or noticing every mistake. Even when I have something helpful to say, I stay quiet. Social interactions drain me, and I often leave early just to escape the pressure. It’s starting to affect my confidence.

I can see how overwhelming it must be for you to feel like you're always under scrutiny at work. It sounds like these experiences are really impacting your self-confidence and overall well-being. Let's explore this further—what goes through your mind during these social interactions? What thoughts come up that make you hesitant to speak up?

Yeah... I guess the main thought is that whatever I say is going to reveal that I don't really belong here. Like, if I stay quiet, I can just blend in and no one will notice me, but if I speak, they'll finally see that I'm not as competent as everyone else. I feel like I have to sound perfect or my input isn't valid. And in the moment, my mind just races—I'll start forming a sentence, then second-guess every word, and by the time I've decided it's safe to say something, the conversation has already moved on. Then I just feel frustrated with myself for missing the chance.

Hmm, that's a good question. I think it's worse when the meeting is more informal, actually—like when it's a smaller group or a brainstorming session. In big presentations where everyone's just listening to one person, it's easier to hide. But when it's more conversational and people are expected to throw ideas around, I feel so much pressure to contribute, and that's when I freeze up. And I notice it's especially bad if there are people in the room who I think are really sharp or who have strong personalities. I start comparing myself to them and feeling like my ideas won't measure up. It's like I assume everyone else is more qualified to speak than I am.

Wait, I think you might have accidentally repeated the same question. But that's okay—it's actually a good one to think about more. To answer again... yes, there have been some positive moments. My manager has told me a couple of times that she values my perspective, and one colleague even reached out after a meeting to say they liked a point I made. I guess I just dismissed those moments as people being polite, rather than actually meaning it. Maybe I need to start keeping track of those positive interactions somehow, so when my brain tells me everyone thinks I'm incompetent, I have actual evidence to fight back with.

I think that's a good next step for me. The idea of "observing without jumping to conclusions" is interesting—I usually just assume the worst immediately and don't even give myself a chance to see how people actually react. Maybe I could try in the next small meeting to share one small thought, and then instead of replaying it negatively afterward, I could try to just... notice what actually happened. Like, did anyone roll their eyes? Did someone build on what I said? Did my manager nod? Just collect the facts instead of inventing a disaster. That feels doable. Scary, but doable. And I like that it's more about being curious than about performing perfectly.

Yeah, I think a journal could actually help a lot. I'm the type of person who trusts written proof more than my own memory anyway. If I can look back and see a list of times I contributed and it went fine—or even well—maybe that'll slowly start to override the constant self-doubt. I'll start small. Maybe just a note in my phone after meetings where I speak up, jotting down what I said and how people responded. Nothing fancy. Just facts. And if it feels too hard to write positive things about myself, I could even just write down what others said verbatim, so it's not me praising myself—it's just recording their words. Thank you. This conversation has really helped me see this as something I can work on step by step, not just a permanent flaw in my personality.

cases.title: Relationship Stress
cases.situation: Taylor, a 27-year-old in a long-term romantic relationship, finds themselves caught in frequent arguments with their partner. They feel anxious that these conflicts could lead to a breakup and often ruminate about things said during disagreements. Taylor tends to overanalyze messages and social cues, seeking reassurance from friends, while at other times withdrawing from the relationship to protect themselves emotionally. They feel a mix of frustration, sadness, and guilt, struggling to communicate effectively without escalating tension.
user_turns: I’ve been arguing with my partner a lot lately, and it makes me anxious that our relationship might fall apart. After every disagreement, I replay everything in my head and wonder what I did wrong. I overthink texts and tone, sometimes pulling away to protect myself, other times seeking reassurance. I feel frustrated, sad, and guilty, and I don’t know how to communicate without making things worse.

I can try. The last argument we had was about something small, honestly—it was about plans for the weekend. I thought we had agreed to keep it free, and they made plans with friends without checking with me first. It started off okay, but then they said I was being controlling, and I just... shut down. I didn't yell or anything. I just got really quiet and said "it's fine" even though it wasn't. Then later that night, I sent a text asking if they were mad at me, and they said they were tired and we'd talk tomorrow. And I just lay there replaying everything, wondering if I was actually being controlling, or if I overreacted, or if this is going to turn into a huge thing. The pattern is usually the same—something small triggers it, one of us gets defensive, and then I either go silent or start anxiously seeking reassurance. I hate it.

I think if I talked more openly in the moment, maybe things wouldn't build up the way they do. Like with the weekend plans—if I had just said "Hey, I'm a little disappointed because I thought we were going to keep the weekend open," instead of saying "it's fine" and shutting down, maybe they wouldn't have felt attacked and called me controlling. But honestly, the reason I shut down is because I'm scared that if I express disappointment, it'll turn into a fight. So I tell myself it's safer to just swallow it. But then it comes out sideways later—either in my anxious texts or in the way I act distant—and that probably confuses them even more. I guess I need to learn how to say things calmly before the resentment builds. It's just hard in the moment when I feel that pit in my stomach.

Yes, I would. I think I swing between two extremes—either I say nothing and bottle it up, or I get anxious and start seeking reassurance in a way that probably comes across as clingy or needy. I don't really have a middle ground where I can just calmly and clearly say what I need. What does assertive communication actually look like in practice? Like, if I'm feeling disappointed about something, how do I say that without it sounding like an accusation or without making my partner defensive?

That actually feels really doable. When you phrase it like that, I can see how it would land differently. Saying "I feel disappointed" is just me owning my emotion—it's not blaming them or attacking their choice. They can't really argue with how I feel, you know? It's just my truth. I think part of why I struggle is that in my head, expressing a need feels like I'm being demanding. Like if I say I'm disappointed, I'm implying they did something wrong. But I guess that's not true—I can be disappointed without them having done anything wrong. It's just... two things can be true at once. I want to try using more "I" statements. Do you have any tips for staying calm while I'm saying them? Sometimes my voice shakes or I start tearing up, and then I feel embarrassed and just want to disappear.

Yeah, the deep breathing thing could help. I notice that when I start to feel that panic, my chest gets tight and I stop breathing properly—I probably sound even more shaky and upset because I'm not getting enough air. Maybe before I start a conversation like this, I could take a few deep breaths and even remind myself that it's okay to feel nervous. And if my voice shakes or I tear up... maybe that's not the end of the world. It might even show my partner that I really care, instead of making me look weak like I always assume. I also like the idea of reflecting on past successes. I can't think of any off the top of my head, but maybe if I start practicing this, I'll be able to look back and say "that conversation went better than I expected." That could build some confidence over time.

It does, yeah. I think setting aside specific times could actually help a lot—right now, a lot of our arguments happen when one of us is tired or stressed or distracted, and it's just bad timing. If we both knew we had a dedicated time to talk things through, maybe we wouldn't feel so pressured to resolve everything in the moment when emotions are high. And the empathy part... I think I need to remember that they're probably struggling too. When I shut down, they might feel frustrated or rejected. When they get defensive, it might be because they feel attacked or misunderstood. We're both just trying to protect ourselves, I guess. I want to try suggesting a weekly check-in with them—just 15 minutes where we can talk about anything that's been on our minds, without it being a fight. Maybe that would take the pressure off.

That sounds really good. Honestly, just talking through this has helped me feel less alone and less like something is fundamentally wrong with me or the relationship. I can see now that it's more about building skills and creating better habits together—not about fixing some huge flaw. I feel like I have some actual tools now: using "I" statements, taking deep breaths before tough talks, suggesting a weekly check-in, and remembering that my partner and I are on the same team even when we disagree. Thank you for helping me break this down. I was feeling so stuck and scared before, and now I at least have a direction to move in.

cases.title: Workplace Burnout
cases.situation: Morgan, a 35-year-old project manager, has been experiencing prolonged stress at work due to an unmanageable workload and high expectations. They feel constantly exhausted, emotionally drained, and struggle to find motivation to complete daily tasks. Morgan has started skipping meals, working late into the night, and neglecting self-care routines such as exercise or hobbies. Irritability and feelings of hopelessness have begun spilling into personal life, causing tension with family and friends.
user_turns: I feel completely overwhelmed at work. The workload never ends, and I’m exhausted all the time. I’ve been skipping meals, staying up late to finish tasks, and I hardly have energy for anything outside of work. I’m irritable, drained, and starting to feel hopeless. It’s affecting my family and my ability to function.

Thank you for all of that. I know you're giving me good advice, and I appreciate it—I really do. It's just... I've heard a lot of this before, and in theory, I know it's what I should be doing. But when I'm in the thick of it, I can't seem to make myself do any of it. It's like my brain just freezes. Even the idea of making a to-do list feels overwhelming right now because I look at everything and I don't even know where to start. And delegating—I don't even know how to begin that conversation without feeling like I'm admitting failure. I'm scared that if I go to my boss and say I need help, they'll see me as weak or incapable. I've built my whole reputation on being reliable and handling things, and the thought of losing that is terrifying.

It's like... part of me hears what you're saying, and I want to believe it. That asking for help could be seen as resourceful instead of weak. But there's this voice in my head that's been telling me for years that I have to handle everything on my own, and it's really hard to quiet that voice. When you talk about breaking things down into smaller pieces, I think that could help. Even just saying it out loud—maybe I don't have to fix everything all at once. Maybe I just need to figure out what one small thing I can do tomorrow. But even that feels hard right now because everything is so jumbled in my head. And mindfulness... I've heard of it, but I'll be honest, the idea of sitting still with my thoughts sounds kind of terrifying. My mind is just racing all the time. When I try to slow down, it almost makes the anxiety worse because then I'm not distracting myself with work. Does that make sense?

Thank you for understanding about the mindfulness piece. That idea of just focusing on my breathing for a few minutes at a time feels... maybe doable. Not as scary as sitting there for a long time with my thoughts. I think I could try that—maybe set a little reminder on my phone to just stop and take a few deep breaths. And okay, picking one small thing for today. Let me think. I have this report that's been sitting on my desk for three days. Every time I look at it, I feel this wave of dread because it's going to take focus and I'm already exhausted. But maybe I don't have to finish it today. Maybe I could just... open it. Read the first paragraph. That's it. Just open it and read the first few sentences. Is that too small? It feels almost silly to call that a step, but right now, even opening it feels like something I've been avoiding.

It helps to hear that—that it's okay to start that small. I think I've been putting so much pressure on myself to fix everything at once that I forget I can just... take one tiny step. I'm going to try it. Later today, when I have a few minutes, I'll open that report and just read the first paragraph. That's it. No pressure to do more. And I'll try the breathing thing too—maybe just once today, set a timer for two minutes and focus on my breath. That feels like something I could actually do without it overwhelming me. Thank you for not making me feel like I have to have it all figured out right now. That alone takes some of the weight off. I'll let you know how it goes.

cases.title: Grief
cases.situation: Anna, a 40-year-old, recently lost a close family member and is struggling to cope with the profound grief. They experience frequent tearfulness, intrusive memories, and difficulty concentrating on daily responsibilities. Anna feels an overwhelming sense of emptiness and guilt about things left unsaid or undone. Social interactions feel draining, and they often isolate themselves from friends and colleagues. Sleep disturbances and loss of appetite have compounded their emotional pain.
user_turns: Since losing my family member, everything feels heavy. I get emotional out of nowhere, and memories keep hitting me when I least expect it. I can barely focus on daily tasks, and I’ve been isolating myself because social interactions take too much energy. I feel empty, guilty, and like I don’t know how to move forward.

Thank you. I know you're trying to be helpful, and I appreciate that. I just… I don't think it's a medical thing. It's grief. It's been like this since the funeral—the waves keep coming, and I can't predict when they'll hit. I've thought about support groups, but the idea of being around people right now, even online, feels exhausting. I don't have the energy to explain myself or to hear other people's stories when I can barely carry my own.

I hear what you're saying about writing things down. I used to journal years ago, before all this. Maybe that's something I could try again—just getting it out of my head, even if no one else reads it. The boundaries thing is harder, though. When people reach out—coworkers, friends—they mean well. They ask how I'm doing, and I don't know what to say. If I'm honest, it makes them uncomfortable. If I say "I'm fine," I feel like I'm lying to myself and to them. Most days I just avoid the situation entirely by not answering. I guess I'm still figuring out how to exist in the world when inside I feel so broken.

That idea of saying something honest but also setting a boundary—I hadn't really thought of that. Like, "I'm having a hard day, but I need some quiet time right now." That feels... truer than "I'm fine," but it also gives me an out so I don't have to get into all of it. I think I could try that. It's just hard because I don't want to push people away completely. I'm scared that if I keep isolating myself, eventually they'll stop reaching out. And then I'll really be alone. But right now, being around people feels like too much. You mentioned finding things that bring me joy. That's the thing—nothing really does right now. Things I used to love just feel hollow. I'll try them and just end up thinking about her, or feeling guilty for enjoying myself when she's gone. It's like joy and grief can't exist in the same space.

Thank you. I think I needed to hear that progress doesn't have to be linear. I've been measuring myself against some imaginary timeline—like by now I should be feeling better, should be back to normal. But there is no normal anymore, is there? There's just... a new way of being. I like the idea of practicing communication. That honest-but-boundaried line we talked about—"I'm having a heavy day, but I need some quiet"—that feels like something I could actually say. Maybe I'll try it with one person this week. Just one. See how it feels. And the mindfulness... I'm still a little nervous about it, but I think I understand it better now. Not as sitting with the pain, but as just... being present. Even for a minute. That feels doable. I'm scared, honestly. Scared that if I let myself feel too much, I'll drown in it. But I'm also scared of staying stuck in this numb, heavy place forever. So I'll keep trying. One small step at a time.

I'll try to keep that in mind—that setbacks aren't failures, they're just part of it. That's hard for me to believe right now, but maybe if I hear it enough times, it'll start to sink in. Thank you. For all of this. For not rushing me, for giving me actual things to try, for making me feel like I'm not broken—just grieving. I'm going to hold onto that.

cases.title: Low Self-esteem
cases.situation: Riley, a 19-year-old university student, consistently struggles with self-doubt and negative self-talk. They feel unworthy in social settings and fear judgment from peers, often avoiding opportunities to participate in group projects or social activities. Riley frequently criticizes their own abilities, comparing themselves unfavorably to others, and experiences persistent anxiety about making mistakes. This lack of confidence affects both academic performance and social relationships, leaving them feeling isolated.
user_turns: I constantly feel like I’m not good enough. In social situations or group projects, I worry that people are judging me, so I usually avoid participating. I compare myself to others and always come up short. I get anxious about making mistakes and it affects my academics and relationships. I feel isolated and full of self-doubt.

(crying softly) I've tried telling myself positive things, but it feels fake. Like I'm lying to myself. And when I do try to join conversations, I just end up overthinking everything I say afterward, convinced I said something stupid. My group project partner probably thinks I'm useless \- I couldn't even speak up during our presentation.

(looking up slightly) I didn't know there might be free options... maybe I could look into what my university offers. (pauses, then speaks more quietly) It's just... even the thought of reaching out for help makes me feel like I'm admitting defeat, you know? Like everyone else can handle life but I'm too weak.

(a small, tentative smile appears) That... actually sounds doable. Not easy, but doable. (fidgets with their sleeve again but seems slightly calmer) Maybe I could even bring a book to the cafeteria, so I have something to focus on besides feeling like everyone's watching me.

(thinking for a moment) I think... I'm scared that even if I try, I'll just fail and prove to myself that I really am as useless as I think. But I guess... not trying at all is already failing, isn't it? (takes a deep breath) I'll check the counseling website tonight. And maybe tomorrow, I'll try the cafeteria for just 10 minutes.
(a genuine smile now, though still shy) Thank you... for listening and not making me feel crazy for feeling this way. I'll let you know how it goes.

cases.title: Perfectionism
cases.situation: Casey, a 21-year-old student, is obsessed with achieving perfect grades and often feels paralyzed by the fear of making mistakes. They spend excessive time revising assignments, double-checking work, and avoiding leisure activities to meet their self-imposed standards. Casey experiences frequent anxiety, guilt, and frustration when outcomes are not flawless. This perfectionism also affects relationships, as they struggle to delegate tasks or accept constructive feedback.
user_turns: I feel like everything I do has to be perfect. I spend hours revising assignments and checking every detail because I’m terrified of making mistakes. Even small imperfections make me feel guilty or frustrated. It’s taking over my time, affecting my relationships, and I can’t relax because I’m always thinking about what I could do better.

It's always kind of been there, but it got so much worse when I started university. Everything feels like it matters more now—like if I mess up, it's going to follow me forever. One bad grade could ruin my GPA, and then what if I can't get into grad school, or I can't get a good job? It spirals so fast in my head. I remember in high school, I could still let things go sometimes. I'd finish an assignment and hand it in, even if it wasn't perfect. Now I'll re-read the same paragraph ten times, change it, change it back, and still feel like it's wrong when I finally submit it. And then I just lie awake thinking about all the things I could have done differently.

It affects everything, honestly. My friends will ask me to hang out, and I'll say no because I "have to study"—but really, I've already studied for hours, I just can't convince myself it's enough. So I stay in my room, staring at the same notes, while they're out having fun. And then I feel guilty for missing out, but I also feel guilty for even wanting to go. Even when I'm not working, I'm thinking about work. I'll be trying to watch a show or eat dinner, and my brain is just running through checklists: Did I cite that correctly? Should I email my professor about that one comment? What if I misunderstood the assignment? And group projects are the worst. I hate relying on other people because they don't do things the way I would. I end up redoing their work or just doing it all myself, and then I resent them for it, but I also can't bring myself to trust them with it. It's exhausting.

I haven't really told them how bad it's gotten. My parents—they're proud of me. I'm the first one in my family to go to university, and they've always said things like, "You're so smart," "You work so hard," "You're going to do great things." And I don't want to disappoint them. I don't want them to think I can't handle it, or that they were wrong to believe in me. Sometimes my mom will ask why I look so tired, and I just say, "Lots of schoolwork." Which is true, but it's not the whole truth. If I told her I was lying awake for hours rethinking a single sentence, I don't know if she'd understand. She'd probably just tell me to relax, like it's that simple. So I just... keep it to myself. Smile and say I'm fine.

Yeah... actually, I did. I got a paper back yesterday—it was an A-minus. And instead of being relieved or proud, all I could focus on was the "minus." I immediately started thinking about what I could have done differently, what the professor didn't like, why it wasn't good enough. It's like my brain just erases anything that isn't perfect and zeroes in on the flaw. And you're right, it's all-or-nothing. If it's not flawless, it's a failure. There's no in-between. I know logically that's not true—I'd tell a friend the same thing—but for myself, I can't seem to accept it.

I think... it started really early. In elementary school, I remember getting a 98 on a test and my teacher asked, "What happened to the other two points?" She was probably joking, but I never forgot it. It stuck with me—like even 98 wasn't enough. And my parents, they never punished me for bad grades or anything. But they always made a big deal out of the good ones. Like, "Look at Casey, always so smart, always getting As." And I think somewhere along the way, I decided that if I wasn't getting As, I wasn't being who they thought I was. Like my value was tied to that. In high school, I was the "smart kid." That was my identity. And now in university, everyone's smart. Everyone's getting good grades. So I feel like I have to do more, be better, just to stand out—or even just to keep up. If I'm not excelling, what am I?

That's... really hard to wrap my head around, honestly. I've spent so long thinking of grades as a measure of me—like if the work is perfect, then I'm valuable, and if it's not, I'm not. So separating my worth from the outcome feels almost impossible. But when you put it that way—"a wish to improve rather than a reflection of your intelligence"—it does sound a little different. Like maybe the A-minus isn't saying I'm not smart enough. Maybe it's just saying there's room to grow, which is... normal. Everyone has room to grow. It's just hard to believe it when that voice in my head is so loud.

I think I'm willing to try. It's scary, though—like if I stop holding myself to this impossible standard, what if I just... stop trying altogether? What if I become lazy or complacent? That thought terrifies me. But I also know that the way I'm living right now isn't sustainable. I'm exhausted, I'm isolated, and I'm never satisfied. So something has to change. Maybe starting small—like, when I notice myself spiraling over a tiny mistake, I could try to ask myself: "Would I judge a friend this harshly for this?" That might help me get some distance.

Yeah, I think I would. It's not going to change overnight, but maybe if I just keep asking that question—"Would I say this to a friend?"—eventually it'll start to feel less automatic, this harsh voice. I'll try it this week. Next time I catch myself re-reading a paragraph for the tenth time or spiraling over a comment, I'll pause and ask that. It might feel weird at first, but... I'm willing to see what happens.

cases.title: Depressive Episode
cases.situation: Sam, a 45-year-old accountant, has been feeling a profound sense of hopelessness for several weeks. They have lost all motivation for work and hobbies, describing each day as "a gray, heavy fog." Sam's appetite has decreased, leading to unintended weight loss, and they sleep for long hours but never feel rested. They are plagued by thoughts of being a failure and often find themselves staring into space, unable to concentrate on their work. Sam has started making excuses to avoid social commitments, preferring to stay in bed
user_turns: For weeks now, I’ve felt this deep sense of hopelessness. It’s like every day is covered in a gray fog. I’ve lost interest in everything I used to enjoy, and even basic tasks feel impossible. I’m not eating much, I sleep a lot but never feel rested, and I can’t concentrate at work. I just feel like a failure and want to withdraw from everyone.

I... I'm safe. I'm not going to hurt myself, if that's what you're asking. It's more like... I just don't see the point. I'm not actively suicidal, I just feel so empty and tired all the time. I know you're worried, and I appreciate that. I've thought about reaching out to someone, but even picking up the phone feels like too much right now. I don't know what they could even say.

I don't even know where to start. Everything feels equally impossible. The thought of going to work makes me nauseous, but the thought of calling in sick again makes me feel guilty. I haven't touched my guitar in months—I used to play every weekend. Now it just sits in the corner collecting dust. Maybe... maybe that's something? I don't know if I could play it, but just looking at it makes me sad. Like I'm mourning the person I used to be.

It sounds manageable when you say it like that. But my brain keeps telling me that even small things won't matter, so why bother? That voice is really loud. But... I hear what you're saying about breaking it down. Maybe I don't have to play the guitar. Maybe I just... sit near it. Or pick it up and hold it without even trying to play. That feels less terrifying than expecting myself to just pick up where I left off. And work... I don't know. Every task feels monumental. But maybe I could just focus on getting through one hour at a time instead of the whole day.

I think I could try that. Just... sitting with it. Not expecting anything. That feels like less pressure. And maybe for work, I'll try the one-hour thing. Just get through this hour, then the next. I've been so focused on getting through the whole day that I exhaust myself before I even start. It's still hard. The fog is still there. But having something to try—even something small—makes me feel like I'm not just sinking. Thank you for that.

I will. That means more than you know—just having someone to talk to who doesn't expect me to be okay right away. I'll try the guitar this week. And the one-hour chunks. And maybe... maybe I'll try eating something small today, even if I'm not hungry. Just to say I did. Thank you for listening. I'll be here next time.

cases.title: Depression with Irritability
cases.situation: Asher, a 38-year-old retail manager, is experiencing a depressed mood that manifests primarily as irritability and anger. They have a short fuse with employees, family, and even customers, reacting with disproportionate frustration to minor inconveniences. Underneath the anger, Asher feels a constant, heavy sadness and believes that no one understands what they are going through. They feel agitated and restless, have trouble falling asleep, and are deeply critical of themselves for their inability to "snap out of it."
user_turns: Lately, I feel constantly on edge and irritated, even over small things. I snap at people—employees, family, customers—and then feel terrible afterward. Underneath the anger, there’s this heavy sadness I can’t shake. I can’t sleep well, I’m restless, and I keep blaming myself for not being able to ‘get it together.

(sighs heavily) I don't even know where to start with that. When I say "get it together," I mean... I'm a grown man. I'm supposed to be able to handle stress. I manage a whole store, I have a family, I have responsibilities. And I'm over here losing my temper because someone left a cart in the wrong spot or my kid left a light on. It's humiliating. I see the way people look at me after I snap—like they're walking on eggshells—and I hate it. I hate myself for it. Triggers? Everything. Nothing. I'll be fine one minute and then something tiny happens and I just... explode. And then the sadness hits right after, like a wave. It's like I'm angry at the world and then angry at myself for being angry. I've tried the deep breathing stuff. My wife bought me an app. But when I'm in that moment, I can't think about breathing. I can't think at all. I just react. And then later I'm lying in bed at 2 a.m. replaying it all, hating myself, and I can't shut my brain off.

(crosses arms, then uncrosses them—can't seem to get comfortable) Yeah, okay. That... actually makes some sense. What goes through my mind right before I snap? Usually it's something like, "Why can't anyone just do things right?" or "Now I have to fix this too." Like I'm already carrying so much, and every little thing someone else does wrong feels like another weight on my back. And yeah, afterward it's definitely "I'm such a jerk" or "What's wrong with me?" I don't give myself any grace at all. The sleep thing... I've tried cutting out coffee after dinner. Doesn't seem to help. My brain just won't shut up. My wife will be asleep next to me and I'm just staring at the ceiling, replaying every stupid thing I said that day. I guess I'm open to trying something. I'm tired of feeling like this. Tired of being tired. Tired of being the guy everyone's afraid to talk to.

(rubs the back of his neck, thinking) That's hard to hear—that the outbursts don't define me. Because in the moment, they feel like all of me. But I get what you're saying. When I see one of my employees mess up, I don't think they're a bad person. I just think they made a mistake. I don't give myself that same courtesy. Maybe if I could catch myself sooner—before it gets to that point—I could... I don't know, step back. But it happens so fast. The wind-down thing... I could try it. My wife's been after me to put the phone down at night anyway. Maybe I read instead. Or just sit in the dark for a bit. Feels weird to schedule that, but if it helps me stop lying there hating myself at 2 a.m., I'll try anything at this point.

I think both are connected, aren't they? If I could wind down better at night, maybe I wouldn't be so on edge during the day. And if I could catch myself earlier, maybe I wouldn't have so much to replay at night. But if I have to pick one to start with... let's try the catching myself. Because that's the part that's wrecking my relationships. My wife shouldn't have to walk on eggshells. My kids shouldn't be scared to talk to me. What does that even look like, though? How do I catch something that feels like it happens in a split second?

Yeah. I can try that. I think the hardest part is gonna be remembering to do it in the moment. But maybe if I just start with noticing—like, after it happens, even if I didn't catch it in time, I could mentally note, "Okay, that was a trigger. The tightness in my chest started right before I snapped." Maybe over time I'll get faster at recognizing it. My wife will probably be surprised if I suddenly start walking away in the middle of an argument. But she'd probably prefer that to me yelling. I'll give it a shot. What've I got to lose at this point?

cases.title: Chronic, Low-Grade Depression
cases.situation: Rowan, a 29-year-old writer, has felt "down" for as long as they can remember.This isn't an intense sadness, but a constant, low-grade hum of gloom and low self-esteem. They describe themselves as naturally pessimistic and have little faith in their own abilities. Rowan functions well enough to meet deadlines but feels chronically inadequate and derives little joy from their successes. They have a few close friends but often feel like a burden, and their social life is limited as a result
user_turns: I’ve felt low for as long as I can remember. It’s not overwhelming sadness, but this constant dull gloom that never goes away. I function well enough, but I don’t really feel joy or pride in my accomplishments. I often feel inadequate and like a burden to others, so I keep my social life small. It just feels like this is my default state.

I've never heard that term before—dysthymia. It's strange to think that this... this fog I've always known might actually have a name. I've tried some of the things you mentioned. Exercise, eating well. I do them, and they're fine, but they don't really change the underlying feeling. It's like putting a bandage on something that's always there. The beliefs about myself... I don't even know where to start with that. I've always just assumed I'm not as good as other people. When I finish a piece of writing, I don't feel proud—I just feel relieved that no one noticed how flawed it is. And with friends, I'm always waiting for them to realize they're better off without me.

(reflects for a moment) I hear what you're saying about reframing, but I have to be honest—when I try to tell myself something positive, it feels like I'm lying. Like I'm just putting on a costume. The negative thoughts feel truer, even if they're painful. I've thought about therapy before. It's just... hard to justify, I guess? I'm functioning. I'm not in crisis. There are people who have it so much worse. Part of me feels like I should just be able to handle this on my own.

The idea of a safe space to express myself without judgment... that does sound appealing. I don't really have that anywhere else. With friends, I'm always filtering, always trying to be the version of me that isn't a burden. Challenging negative thoughts... I'm willing to try, but I'll need help with it. I've been thinking this way for so long, I don't even know what "normal" thinking looks like. I guess I'm starting to realize that just because I'm functioning doesn't mean I'm okay. Maybe I've been telling myself that for years to avoid having to face this.

Yeah. I think I could do that. It feels a little vulnerable, putting it down on paper—actually seeing the thoughts I usually just let swirl around in my head. But maybe that's the point. Maybe if I see them written out, they'll look less like facts and more like... just thoughts. I'll start this week. Just jot down when that "I'm a burden" feeling comes up, or when I finish something and feel nothing but relief. See if I can catch any patterns. And I'll think more about the therapy idea. It's still hard to give myself permission, but... I'm getting there.
